mainTopic: Writing a שובר (receipt) when a loan document is lost, and how postdated (שטר מאוחר) loan and sale documents can be misused and protected.
overview: The גמרא explains that רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי argue only about an ordinary שטר מאוחר, and that each follows his own view on writing a שובר. רבי יהודה says we do not write a שובר, so a late date is harmless. רבי יוסי says we do write one, so a late date could let a lender collect twice. רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע limits the שובר to partial payment, but the גמרא rejects this: a שובר is written even for full payment. It proves this from a court case before רבי חנינא בר פפי, from רבי יוחנן, ריש לקיש and רבי אילעא, and from fairness, and רבא answers אביי that "the borrower is a servant to the lender." Next a משנה rules that antedated loan documents are invalid and postdated ones are valid. רב המנונא says postdated sale documents are invalid because of a buy-back trick. Loans are safe, he says, because he holds we do not write a שובר. Since in practice both are written, רב כהנא cites the fixes of רבי אבא and רב ספרא for the wording of the document and of the receipt, and another question begins that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The dispute is only about an ordinary postdated document
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא narrows the argument between רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי. It is only about a regular שטר מאוחר.
steps.simpleTranslation: They only disagree about an ordinary postdated document.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is pinning down exactly what רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי argue about. This sets up the next two steps, which give each side's reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An ordinary שטר מאוחר is one where nothing in the date shows that it was written late. That is different from a document dated on a day like שבת, when no one writes documents. The argument is only about the hidden kind, because only there can a late date fool a court.

keyTerms.meaning: they disagreed
a loan document dated later than the day it was really written
in general; an ordinary, plain case

steps.confusionAlert: A שטר מאוחר is dated LATER than the real loan date. Do not mix it up with a שטר מוקדם, which is dated EARLIER.

phrases.english: They disagree only
about an ordinary postdated document –
phrases.notes: "Ordinary" means you cannot tell from the date itself that the document was written late.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא נֶחְלְקוּ אֶלָּא בִּשְׁטָר מְאוּחָר בְּעָלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the scope of the רבי יהודה / רבי יוסי dispute from the earlier part of the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The dispute is limited to an ordinary שטר מאוחר, where the late dating cannot be seen from the date.

steps.title: רבי יהודה's reason: no receipts, so no harm
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה holds that we do not write a שובר. So a late date on a שטר cannot cause any harm.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה follows his own reasoning, since he says we do not write a receipt. So no harm can come from a postdated document.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains רבי יהודה's view. He sees no danger in a postdated document, because he does not allow a שובר to be written.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we never write a שובר, then when a loan is paid the שטר itself is torn up. If only part is paid, a new שטר is written for the rest. Since there is no separate receipt, there is never a dated receipt that a late שטר could seem to come after. So a late date cannot be used to cheat.

keyTerms.meaning: following his own reasoning, as he said elsewhere
a receipt showing that a debt was paid
harm, damage

phrases.english: For Rabbi Yehuda follows his reasoning,
as he says: We do not write a receipt,
and so no harm comes out of it;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first side's reasoning for the dispute defined in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהודה, we do not write a שובר, so a שטר מאוחר causes no harm.

steps.title: רבי יוסי's reason: receipts are written, so harm can result
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי holds that we do write a שובר. A late date on the שטר could then make the שובר look as if it came before the loan.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי follows his own reasoning, since he says we do write a receipt. So harm can come from a postdated document.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains רבי יוסי's view. He sees danger in a postdated document, because he allows a שובר to be written instead of tearing the שטר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here is the danger. The loan was given on the 1st of ניסן and paid back on the 2nd, and a שובר dated the 2nd was written. If the שטר says the 3rd, the lender can say the שובר is from before this loan and collect again. That trick only works if receipts exist, which is why רבי יוסי worries about it.

keyTerms.meaning: we write
comes out of it; results from it

steps.whatToRemember: The whole argument about a שטר מאוחר depends on one question: do we write a שובר? No receipts (רבי יהודה) means no danger. Receipts allowed (רבי יוסי) means a late date can be used to collect twice.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yosei follows his reasoning,
as he says: We write a receipt,
and so harm can come out of it.
phrases.notes: The receipt could carry an earlier date than the late loan document, so the lender might try to collect twice.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite side's reasoning, which completes the explanation of the dispute.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יוסי, we write a שובר, so a שטר מאוחר can cause harm.

steps.title: Receipts are written only for partial payment
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע limits the view that we write a שובר. It applies only when part of the debt is paid, not all of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא son of רב יהושע says: Even according to the one who says we write a receipt, that is only for half of the debt. For all of it, no.
steps.whatsHappening: A new אמורא adds a limit to the view that we write a שובר. He says receipts are written only for a partial payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the borrower pays only part, a שובר makes sense, since the lender still needs his שטר for the rest. But if the borrower pays everything and the lender cannot produce the שטר, we do not write a שובר. The borrower simply does not have to pay until the שטר is brought and torn up.

keyTerms.meaning: according to the one who says
these words apply only to; this rule is limited to
on half, meaning a partial payment
on all of it, meaning full payment

steps.whyThisMatters: According to רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע, even the side that allows receipts would not allow one for full payment, so a borrower paying in full could insist on getting the שטר back. The next step rejects this limit.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ:
phrases.english: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua said:
Even according to the one who says we write a receipt,
phrases.notes: This is רבי יוסי's view from the step before.

phrases.english: this applies only to half,
phrases.notes: "Half" just means part of the debt, not exactly fifty percent.

phrases.english: but for all of it – no.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ: אֲפִילּוּ לְמַאן דְּאָמַר כּוֹתְבִין שׁוֹבָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the view stated in step 3 (we write a שובר) and limits how far it reaches.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even the view that allows a שובר allows it only for partial payment. For full payment, no שובר is written.

steps.title: Rejecting the partial-payment limit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects רב הונא בריה דרב יהושע: a שובר is written even when the whole debt is paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: But that is not so. We write a receipt even when all of the debt is paid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the limit from the last step. It says a שובר is written even when the full debt is paid, not only part of it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 4 limited writing a שובר to cases of partial payment. Here the גמרא says that limit is wrong: the rule applies to full payment too. The next steps bring the proof.

keyTerms.meaning: But it is not so: a formula that rejects the previous statement
On all of it, meaning the whole debt
We write

phrases.english: But it is not so;
we write [a receipt] even for all of it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the limit given in step 4.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The limit that a שובר is written only for partial payment.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: In practice a שובר is written even when the debt is fully paid.

steps.title: A court case: the lender lost the note
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a story: a lender lost his שטר, and he offered to write a שובר instead so the borrower would pay the full debt.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like the case of רב יצחק בר יוסף, who was owed money by רבי אבא. He came before רבי חנינא בר פפי and said to him: 'Give me my money.' רבי אבא answered: 'Give me back my note, and then take your money.' He replied: 'Your note got lost. I will write you a receipt instead.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a story to prove its point. This step sets up the case; the argument and the ruling come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower wants the שטר back so it can't be used against him again. The lender lost it, so he offers a שובר instead. Notice that this is a full payment of the debt. So if the court allows a שובר here, that proves step 5.

keyTerms.meaning: Was owed money by him
Got lost
A receipt; another word for שובר
A loan document (promissory note)

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דְּרַב יִצְחָק בַּר יוֹסֵף
phrases.english: Like this case of Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef,

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה מַסֵּיק בֵּיהּ זוּזִי בְּרַבִּי אַבָּא.
phrases.english: who was owed money by Rabbi Abba.

phrases.aramaic: אֲתָא לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא בַּר פַּפֵּי,
phrases.english: He came before Rabbi Chanina bar Pappi,
[and] said to him: "Give me my money."
phrases.notes: The lender is speaking to the borrower, רבי אבא.

phrases.english: He said to him: "Give me my note,"
"and take your money."
He said to him: "Your note got lost on me;"
"I will write you a receipt."

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דְּרַב יִצְחָק בַּר יוֹסֵף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a story that proves step 5.
steps.raayaObject: That a שובר is written even when the full debt is paid.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A case judged by רבי חנינא בר פפי.

steps.title: The borrower objects: רב and שמואל say no receipt
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא objects that רב and שמואל hold that we do not write a שובר.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: 'But don't רב and שמואל both say that we do not write a receipt?'
steps.whatsHappening: Inside the story, the borrower challenges the lender's offer. He quotes two great authorities who say a שובר is not written.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אבא doesn't want to rely on a piece of paper he must keep forever. He cites רב and שמואל, who hold like רבי יהודה's approach that we don't write a שובר. Without one, the lender would have to return the original שטר.

keyTerms.meaning: Both of them
We do not write

phrases.english: He said to him: "But Rav and Shmuel —"
"both of them say: We do not write a receipt!"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The borrower answers the lender's offer within the story.
steps.kashyaTarget: The lender's offer to write a שובר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב and שמואל rule that a שובר is not written, so the borrower can demand the original שטר.

steps.title: The judge rules: we write a receipt
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא בר פפי honors רב and שמואל, but rules like רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש that a שובר is written.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: 'Who would give us some of the dust of רב and שמואל? We would put it on our eyes! But רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש both say that we do write a receipt.'
steps.whatsHappening: The judge answers the borrower. He shows great respect for רב and שמואל, but he rules like other great authorities who say a שובר is written.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The judge does not dismiss רב and שמואל; he praises them. Still, he follows רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש. Since this was a full payment, the ruling proves the point of step 5: a שובר is written even for the whole debt.

keyTerms.meaning: His dust
We would put it on our eyes
We write a receipt

steps.whatToRemember: The court allowed a שובר in a case of full payment. That is the proof that we write a שובר even for the whole debt.

phrases.english: He said: "Who would give us
phrases.notes: The speaker is the judge, רבי חנינא בר פפי.

phrases.english: some of the dust of Rav and Shmuel?
We would put it on our eyes!
phrases.notes: This is a way of saying how much he honors them, even though he won't follow them here.

phrases.aramaic: הָא רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְהָא רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
phrases.english: But here is Rabbi Yochanan and here is Reish Lakish,
who both say: We write a receipt."

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן יָהֵיב לַן מֵעַפְרֵיהּ דְּרַב וּשְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the borrower's objection and decides the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since רב and שמואל say no שובר, the lender must return the שטר.
steps.terutzMaskana: We follow רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש: a שובר is written, even when the full debt is paid.

steps.title: רבין's report: רבי אילעא also says we write a receipt
steps.stepSummary: רבין brings a ruling from רבי אילעא that we write a שובר.
steps.simpleTranslation: And likewise, when רבין came, he said that רבי אילעא says: we write a receipt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds more support. A report from ארץ ישראל says רבי אילעא also rules that we write a שובר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds another authority to the side of רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש. It strengthens the ruling that a שובר is written.

keyTerms.meaning: And likewise
When רבין came (from ארץ ישראל to בבל)

steps.whatToRemember: Another authority supports writing a שובר. The next steps add a logical argument for it and test that argument.

phrases.english: And likewise, when Ravin came,
he said that Rabbi Ilai says:
We write a receipt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another authority who supports the ruling in step 8.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי אילעא, as reported by רבין.

steps.title: Logic shows we should write a receipt
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא argues from fairness that we write a שובר. Otherwise, a lender who lost his שטר could never collect, and the borrower would keep money he owes.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense that we write a receipt. If we did not, then whenever a lender lost his document, the borrower would just keep the money and be happy!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a logical reason to support the view that a שובר is written.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we refused to write a שובר, a lender who lost his שטר would be stuck. He could not collect, because the borrower would fear the lost שטר might turn up and be used to collect a second time. So the borrower would get to keep money he really owes. That outcome is unfair, so writing a שובר makes sense.

keyTerms.meaning: And it makes sense / it stands to reason
A receipt showing a debt was paid
A legal document, here the loan document
The other one should eat and be happy (he gains unfairly)

phrases.english: And it stands to reason that we write a receipt;
for if it would enter your mind
that we do not write a receipt,
then if this one's document is lost,
should the other one eat and rejoice?!
phrases.notes: "This one" is the lender and "the other one" is the borrower, who would get to keep the money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a reasoning argument to the sources already brought for writing a שובר.
steps.raayaObject: The ruling that we write a שובר
steps.raayaSupportSource: Fairness logic: otherwise the borrower keeps money he owes

steps.title: אביי: a receipt can also be lost
steps.stepSummary: אביי points out that the fairness argument works both ways. If the borrower loses his שובר, the lender can collect twice.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי objected: So what, should we write a receipt? Then if the borrower loses his receipt, the lender will eat and rejoice!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges the logic of the last step by showing that writing a שובר also leads to an unfair result.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a שובר, the borrower must guard that paper forever. If he loses it, the lender, who may still have the old שטר, can collect again. So either way someone might lose out. Why should the risk fall on the borrower and not on the lender?

keyTerms.meaning: He objects to it (strongly challenges)
But rather what? (so what is the alternative?)
His receipt

phrases.english: Abaye objects to it:
But rather what, we write a receipt?!
If this one's receipt is lost,
phrases.notes: Now "this one" is the borrower, who holds the receipt.

phrases.english: should the other one eat and rejoice?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the fairness reasoning of step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: The fairness argument for writing a שובר
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same unfairness happens in reverse: if the שובר is lost, the lender can collect twice.

steps.title: רבא: the borrower carries the risk
steps.stepSummary: רבא agrees that one side must take the risk, and says it should be the borrower, quoting "the borrower is a servant to the lender."
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: Yes, the borrower takes the risk, because the verse says "The borrower is a servant to the lender."
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers אביי. Yes, it is right that the borrower carries the risk of losing his שובר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא admits that both choices could hurt someone. The פסוק decides the question: the borrower is the one obligated to the lender. So the lender's interests come first, and the borrower must guard his שובר.

keyTerms.meaning: Yes
The borrower is a servant to the lender

steps.whatToRemember: The הלכה is that we write a שובר. The borrower must guard it, because "the borrower is a servant to the lender."

phrases.english: Rava said to him: Yes,
"The borrower is a servant to the lender."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's objection and closes the שובר discussion.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Accepts the premise but justifies the choice with a פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since both sides could lose, there is no reason to favor the lender.
steps.terutzMaskana: The borrower is subordinate to the lender, so the risk falls on him and we write a שובר.

steps.title: משנה: early-dated loan documents are invalid, late-dated are valid
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting a משנה: loan documents dated earlier than the real date are not valid, and those dated later are valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in a משנה elsewhere: Loan documents that are antedated (dated too early) are not valid, and postdated ones (dated too late) are valid.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic begins. The גמרא quotes a משנה about loan documents with a wrong date, to set up רב המנונא's comment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An early date is dangerous because a lender could use it to take land from buyers who bought from the borrower before the loan really happened. A late date only hurts the lender himself, since his claim starts later. So the late date is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: We learned there (in a משנה in another place)
Loan documents
Antedated, given a date earlier than the real one
Postdated, given a date later than the real one

steps.confusionAlert: "Early" and "late" here mean the date written on the paper compared to the real date of the loan, not when the loan is paid back.

phrases.english: We learned there:
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in שביעית, chapter 10.

phrases.english: Loan documents that are antedated are not valid,
and those that are postdated are valid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new section on antedated and postdated documents. The שובר question comes back into it in steps 17-18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Antedated loan documents are not valid, and postdated ones are valid.

steps.title: רב המנונא: sale documents are invalid even if postdated
steps.stepSummary: רב המנונא says the משנה's leniency for late dates applies only to loan documents. Documents of sale are not valid even with a late date.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב המנונא said: This was taught only about loan documents. But documents of buying and selling are not valid even when postdated.
steps.whatsHappening: רב המנונא limits the משנה. The rule "postdated is valid" works only for loans, not for sales.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה seemed to say any late-dated document is fine. רב המנונא adds a new rule: a document of sale with a late date is not valid. The reason comes in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught this about...
Loan documents
Documents of buying and selling

phrases.english: Rav Hamnuna said:
They taught this only about loan documents,
but documents of buying and selling –
even postdated ones are also not valid.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הַמְנוּנָא: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the משנה from step 13 to loan documents only.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Postdated documents of sale are not valid.

steps.title: Why are postdated sale documents invalid?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the reason behind רב המנונא's rule.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why a late date ruins a sale document. This sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a loan, a late date only hurts the lender, so it is allowed. The question is what danger a late date creates with a sale.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?

phrases.english: What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind step 14.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why a postdated sale document is not valid, when a postdated loan document is valid

steps.title: The buy-back trick a late date allows
steps.stepSummary: A seller sells in ניסן, but the document says תשרי. If the seller buys the land back before תשרי, the buyer can later wave the תשרי document and claim he bought it again.
steps.simpleTranslation: Sometimes a person sells land in ניסן but the document says תשרי. In between, the seller happens to get money and buys the land back. When תשרי comes, the buyer pulls out the document and says: "I bought it back from you again!"
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a case showing how a late-dated sale document can be used to cheat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fake later date makes the old sale look like a new purchase that happened after the seller bought the land back. So the buyer can falsely claim the land is his again. רב המנונא assumes loans do not have this danger. The next step challenges that, and step 18 explains why loans are safe in his view.

keyTerms.meaning: Sometimes
In between (in the meantime)
He takes it out (shows the document)
I bought it back from you again

steps.whatToRemember: Postdated loan documents are valid, but postdated sale documents are not, because the late date can make an old sale look like a new purchase.

phrases.english: Sometimes he sells him land in Nisan
and writes the document for him dated Tishrei,
and money happens to come to the seller in between
and he buys the land back from the buyer,
and when Tishrei arrives, the buyer takes out the document,
and says to him: I bought it back from you again!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A postdated sale document lets the buyer falsely claim he bought the land again after the seller bought it back.

steps.title: The same danger should apply to loan documents
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב המנונא: a late-dated loan document could be misused in the same way as a late-dated sale document.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, loan documents should have the same problem. Sometimes a person borrows in ניסן and the document is dated תשרי. Money comes his way in between, and he pays the loan back early. He asks for his document back, and the lender says, "I lost it," so the lender writes him a receipt. When תשרי comes, the lender takes out the document and says, "This is a new loan you took from me now!"
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב המנונא's reason. The same trick seems possible with a late-dated loan document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 16 the danger was that a late date lets someone claim a second deal happened after the first one ended. Here the גמרא shows the same pattern with a loan: the borrower pays early, and the lender says the document is lost. Later the lender brings out the document and claims its תשרי date proves a new loan. So why is a late date allowed for loans?

keyTerms.meaning: If so; if your reasoning is right
In between; during the time between the two dates
It got lost on me
A receipt showing the debt was paid (literally, a 'breaking' of the document)

phrases.english: If so, loan documents too should be a problem:
Sometimes a person borrows in Nisan
and writes him a document dated Tishrei;
and money happens to come his way in between
and he pays him back,
and he says to him: Give me my document,
and the lender says to him: I lost it,
and he writes him a receipt;
and when its date arrives,
phrases.notes: He means the date written in the document, תשרי.

phrases.english: he takes it out and says to him:
This money you borrowed from me only now!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the reason given in Step 16 against the leniency for loan documents.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב המנונא's distinction between loan documents and sale documents
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The danger in the sale case, a late date making a finished deal look new, can also happen with a loan that is paid early when the lender claims the document is lost.

steps.title: רב המנונא holds that we do not write a receipt
steps.stepSummary: The danger can't happen with loans, because רב המנונא holds that a receipt is not written in place of the returned document.
steps.simpleTranslation: He holds that we do not write a receipt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the loan story can't happen in רב המנונא's view. He holds that a receipt is not written.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The whole trick in Step 17 needed the lender to keep the document and give a receipt instead. If we never write a receipt, the borrower pays only when he gets his document back. Then no document is left over for the lender to misuse. With a sale there is no repayment, so this answer does not help there.

keyTerms.meaning: He holds; it is his opinion
A receipt for a paid debt (same idea as תְּבָרָא)

phrases.english: He holds: We do not write a receipt.
phrases.notes: 'He' is רב המנונא. So the borrower doesn't pay until he gets the actual document back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Removing a needed piece of the problem scenario: no receipt means no leftover document
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Late-dated loan documents should be just as dangerous as late-dated sale documents.
steps.terutzMaskana: Since רב המנונא holds we do not write a receipt, the loan trick can't happen, so late-dated loan documents stay valid.

steps.title: But today we write both late dates and receipts
steps.stepSummary: רב יימר (or רב ירמיה מדיפתי) asks רב כהנא: today we do write late-dated documents and receipts, so how is the danger avoided?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יימר said to רב כהנא, and some say it was רב ירמיה מדיפתי who said it to רב כהנא: Nowadays we write late-dated documents and we also write receipts. Why do we do that?
steps.whatsHappening: A later אמורא points out that the real practice today includes both pieces of the dangerous story. He asks how that can be allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 18 avoided the danger by saying we don't write receipts. But the practice of their time was to write late-dated loan documents and to give receipts when a document was lost. Together these make the trick from Step 17 possible again, so he asks why we act this way.

keyTerms.meaning: And some say; another version of who said it
Nowadays; in our time
Documents dated later than the real date

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב יֵימַר לְרַב כָּהֲנָא,
phrases.english: Rav Yeimar said to Rav Kahana,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ רַב יִרְמְיָה מִדִּיפְתִּי לְרַב כָּהֲנָא:
phrases.english: and some say it was Rav Yirmeya of Difti who said to Rav Kahana:
But nowadays, when we write late-dated documents
and we also write a receipt,
why do we do this?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָאִידָּנָא דְּכָתְבִינַן שְׁטָרֵי מְאוּחָרֵי וְכָתְבִינַן תְּבָרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that Step 18's answer does not fit current practice, which writes receipts.
steps.kashyaTarget: The current practice of writing both late-dated documents and receipts
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Step 17 showed that late dates plus receipts allow a lender to collect twice, and today both are done.

steps.title: רבי אבא's fix: the document admits its late date
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא answers that רבי אבא told his scribes to write in a late-dated document that it was dated late on purpose.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: After רבי אבא told his scribes, "When you write late-dated documents, write this: 'We did not write this document on its date. Rather, we dated it later and wrote it.'"
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא explains that the problem was fixed by a change in the wording of the document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lender's trick works only if the תשרי date looks like the real date of a new loan. Once the document itself says it was dated late, the lender can't use that date to claim a new loan after the repayment. So late dates and receipts can be used together safely.

keyTerms.meaning: After (something happened)
To his scribe(s), the court writer
We made it late; we dated it later

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: The one answering is רב כהנא.

phrases.aramaic: בָּתַר דַּאֲמַר לְהוּ רַבִּי אַבָּא לְסָפְרֵיהּ:
phrases.english: After Rabbi Abba said to his scribes:
When you write late-dated documents,
write like this:
"This document, we did not write it on its date,"
"rather, we dated it later and wrote it."

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּתַר דַּאֲמַר לְהוּ רַבִּי אַבָּא לְסָפְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 19's question about current practice.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A practical fix through added wording in the document
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Writing both late-dated documents and receipts lets a lender collect twice.
steps.terutzMaskana: The document says openly that it was dated late, so its date can't be used to claim a new loan.

steps.title: But today we don't use רבי אבא's wording
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי asks רב כהנא: today scribes don't add רבי אבא's sentence, so how is the danger avoided?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said to רב כהנא: But nowadays, when we don't do this?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי challenges the last answer. In his time scribes no longer add רבי אבא's sentence.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 20's protection depends on the sentence admitting the late date. If scribes stopped writing it, the problem from Step 17 comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: When we don't do this

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אָשֵׁי לְרַב כָּהֲנָא:
phrases.english: Rav Ashi said to Rav Kahana:
But nowadays, when we don't do this?
phrases.notes: 'This' means adding רבי אבא's sentence that the document was dated late.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges Step 20's answer as not matching current practice.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The fix works only if the sentence is written, and scribes no longer write it.

steps.title: רב ספרא's fix: date the receipt correctly or leave it undated
steps.stepSummary: רב ספרא told his scribe to write the document's date in a receipt, or to leave the receipt undated if he didn't know it, so that it always cancels the document.
steps.simpleTranslation: After רב ספרא told his scribe: "When you write these receipts, if you know the date written in the document, write it. If not, write the receipt with no date. Then whenever the document comes out, the receipt will cancel it."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second fix. This time the change is in how the receipt is written, not the loan document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lender's trick depended on the receipt seeming to come before the document's later date. If the receipt names the document's own date, it clearly cancels that document. If the receipt has no date at all, it can't be shown to be earlier than the document. Either way, whenever the lender brings out the document, the receipt weakens it, and he can't collect twice.

keyTerms.meaning: The date written in the document
Plainly, without details; here, with no date
Will weaken it; will cancel its power

steps.whatToRemember: A late date on a loan document is allowed. To stop a lender from collecting twice, either the document says it was dated late (רבי אבא), or the receipt carries the document's date or no date at all (רב ספרא).
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how the חכמים allowed a useful practice, late-dated loan documents, while fixing the scribes' wording so no one could cheat with it.

phrases.aramaic: בָּתַר דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב סָפְרָא לְסָפְרֵיהּ:
phrases.english: After Rav Safra said to his scribe:
When you write these receipts,
if you know the date of the document, write it,
if not, write it plainly, with no date,
so that whenever the document comes out, the receipt will weaken it.

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּתַר דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב סָפְרָא לְסָפְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אשי's challenge in Step 21 with a different fix.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A practical fix through the wording of the receipt
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without רבי אבא's sentence, a late-dated document plus a receipt lets the lender collect twice.
steps.terutzMaskana: A receipt with the document's date, or with no date, cancels the document whenever it is brought out.

steps.title: Introducing the next question about this practice
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא names who asked the next question: רבינא to רב אשי, or, in another version, רב אשי to רב כהנא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רב אשי, and some say it was רב אשי who said to רב כהנא:
steps.whatsHappening: This line only tells us who is about to speak. It sets up the next question, which continues the discussion of רב ספרא's method.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question itself comes right after this line, so here we only learn the speakers. The גמרא gives two versions of who asked whom, which is normal when the tradition about the speakers was not certain.

keyTerms.meaning: He said to him. Often opens a question or a challenge.
And some say it. Introduces a second version of who said something.
An אמורא from the later generations of Babylonian sages, a colleague of רב אשי.

phrases.english: Ravina said to Rav Ashi,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי לַהּ רַב אָשֵׁי לְרַב כָּהֲנָא:
phrases.english: and some say it was Rav Ashi who said to Rav Kahana:

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבִינָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי, וְאָמְרִי לַהּ רַב אָשֵׁי לְרַב כָּהֲנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the next round of questioning after רב ספרא's practice in step 22, following the same pattern as the earlier questions put to רב כהנא in steps 19 and 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The method from step 22 (רב ספרא's practice) for preventing misuse of a late-dated document together with a receipt.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: This line only introduces the speakers. The challenge itself comes on the next amud.
